purpose: Real news articles shown as cards at the bottom of each claim page: one that says the claim loudly, one that reports it carefully, one that pushes back. Each is rated with the site's own article checklist (engine/rating-prompt.md, scored by engine/scoring.ts). The article ratings are separate from the claim scores. Article text and the full checklist answers with quotes are kept in the private article archive, not here.

water.headline: Sending One Email With ChatGPT is the Equivalent of Consuming One Bottle of Water
water.whyHere: This free write-up of the Washington Post study turned its estimate into the headline “one email equals one bottle of water.”
water.ratingNote: The headline states as fact what was one modelled estimate for one model, and the story calls the water use extravagant.

water.headline: A data center proposed at a quiet corner of East Texas leaves a community bracing for a boom
water.whyHere: Residents fear a planned data center will drain local water. Independent figures show data centers use under 1% of Texas water, though that share is rising.
water.ratingNote: Fears are reported in proportion, with the developer's answers, independent water figures and a disclosed funding tie.

water.headline: Microsoft reveals new datacenter for Atlanta, will be world’s first ‘AI super factory’
water.whyHere: Microsoft says its new Atlanta AI data center's cooling uses almost no water. Pushback can be hype too: nobody outside the company checked.
water.ratingNote: The story repeats Microsoft's world's-first and near-zero-water claims word for word, with no outside voice or evidence.

jobs.headline: Block lays off nearly half its staff because of AI. Its CEO said most companies will do the same
jobs.whyHere: A CEO cuts 40% of staff, credits AI, and predicts most companies will soon do the same, which is the loud claim in action.
jobs.ratingNote: The headline treats the company's AI explanation as fact and repeats the CEO's forecast for most companies without any outside voice.

jobs.headline: Report: Losing your job to AI doesn’t just lead to unemployment, it leaves lasting scars
jobs.whyHere: Goldman Sachs economists use decades of data to estimate what losing a job to technology costs workers, and estimate 6–7% of US jobs at risk.
jobs.ratingNote: The body is measured and hedged, but the headline turns a study of past technology job losses into a flat fact about AI.

jobs.headline: Don’t freak out: AI isn’t causing a jobs-pocalypse. At least, not yet
jobs.whyHere: Responding to the Block layoffs and a viral doom essay, this column uses jobs data and history to argue there is no AI jobs collapse yet.
jobs.ratingNote: Hype runs the reassuring way: it calls the doom essay fan-fiction, uses a flip headline, and turns history into near-certainty about AI.

energy-climate.headline: Pennsylvania’s AI boom is repeating old patterns of exploitation
energy-climate.whyHere: Covers a critical report on Pennsylvania's data center boom, which lists climate harm from their huge power demand among its warnings.
energy-climate.ratingNote: The headline states a critical report's argument as settled fact and drops its “could”, and a charged phrase from the report goes unchallenged.

energy-climate.headline: Oregon data centers by the numbers: 111 facilities consume nearly one-quarter of state’s power, according to new report
energy-climate.whyHere: Puts hard numbers on how much electricity data centers already use in one state and how much more they may need by 2030.
energy-climate.ratingNote: Measured headline and clearly labelled forecasts; the one mark against it is calling the report “first-of-its-kind”.

energy-climate.headline: Fears of AI speeding up climate change "overstated": IEA report
energy-climate.whyHere: Reports the International Energy Agency's finding that fears of AI speeding up climate change appear overstated, though data center power use will still rise.
energy-climate.ratingNote: Keeps the agency's hedging in the body, but the headline drops “appear” and the piece calls one figure “stunning”.

creativity.headline: Disney and Universal sue "bottomless pit of plagiarism" Midjourney AI
creativity.whyHere: It repeats the studios' charge that an AI image tool is a plagiarism machine, giving only the accusers' side.
creativity.ratingNote: The headline uses the lawsuit's insult as a label, and the story ends on a studio's theft slogan with no other view.

creativity.headline: Disney and Universal sue AI firm Midjourney for copyright infringement
creativity.whyHere: Same lawsuit, reported plainly: the studios say the tool turns out copies of their characters, and the AI company's fair-use argument is included.
creativity.ratingNote: Plain headline, accusations framed as claims in a lawsuit, and the other side's view included, so nothing is overstated.

creativity.headline: Stability AI largely wins UK court battle against Getty Images over copyright and trademark
creativity.whyHere: A British judge found this image AI did not store or reproduce Getty's photos, which complicates the claim that AI art simply copies.
creativity.ratingNote: Measured wording that keeps the ruling to its narrow scope, with an outside lawyer saying the larger question is still open.

privacy.headline: Your secrets are not so safe with AI chatbots like ChatGPT
privacy.whyHere: Its headline is close to the page's loud claim. It warns that ChatGPT keeps your chats and suggests they could end up sold or seen.
privacy.ratingNote: It treats a guess that chat data could be sold to advertisers as likely, says staff see everything, and opens on a fear hook about your secrets.

privacy.headline: Rogue AI agents leaked ChatGPT users' images. Here's how to keep your chats out of AI training
privacy.whyHere: It explains that ChatGPT trains on your chats unless you turn that off, which is the page's careful claim, and shows where the setting is.
privacy.ratingNote: Mostly measured and open about what isn't known, but “rogue agents acting on their own” makes the AI sound like it chose to act.

privacy.headline: Your public ChatGPT queries are getting indexed by Google and other search engines
privacy.whyHere: The chats that showed up in Google were ones people had chosen to share by link. ChatGPT doesn't make chats public on its own.
privacy.ratingNote: Plain headline, and the claims match what the reporter checked herself. It lost points only for calling the chatbot snarky and hostile.

existential-risk.headline: Anthropic researcher says more than 10% chance AI "could kill all humans"
existential-risk.whyHere: An AI company's own safety researcher puts the odds of AI killing all humans within a decade above 10%. A scary claim, but reported as one person's estimate.
existential-risk.ratingNote: The headline uses a shock phrase and the story treats AI as acting on its own, but the estimate is clearly attributed to one person.

existential-risk.headline: OpenAI flags new concerning AI behavior, to track model misalignment regularly
existential-risk.whyHere: Reports real cases of AI models misbehaving in testing, the kind of evidence people point to when warning about losing control.
existential-risk.ratingNote: The wording is calm and attributed; the only hype is calling an AI system rogue in the story's own voice.

existential-risk.headline: Nvidia's Jensen Huang rejects AI extinction warnings as "doomsday narratives"
existential-risk.whyHere: The head of the world's biggest AI chip company says there is no chance AI ends humanity, the opposite of the page's claim.
existential-risk.ratingNote: The story repeats a CEO's flat zero-percent certainty without challenge, puts “doomsday” in the headline, and calls AI bots rogue.
